title: LLM Judge Validation Under Sparse Overlap: From Inference to Design
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: Under a fixed annotation budget, how labels are allocated biases agreement estimates and drives wrong decisions; shared stratified overlap fixes both.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side: violin plot left, bar chart right, shared color coding
description: Two side-by-side matplotlib plots compare three annotation strategies: depth-first, random spread, and stratified shared. Panel (a), titled 'Human ceiling estimate', is a violin plot of human agreement α̂ on the y-axis. A dashed horizontal line marks the full-data ceiling at about 0.35. Depth-first appears as a single black tick well above the line, near 0.54, which shows bias. Random spread is a wide orange violin spanning roughly -0.3 to 1.0, so it has high variance. Stratified shared is a narrow blue violin tightly centered on the ceiling. Panel (b), titled 'Deployment errors', is a bar chart of wrong decisions in percent. The red depth-first bar is 75%, the orange random-spread bar is 40%, and the blue stratified-shared bar is 26%. The eye goes first to the tall red bar and the wide orange violin.
caption: The same annotation budget can fail in two different ways. On a real visual-assessment task, depth-first labeling biases the human-agreement ceiling (a) and inflates wrong deployment decisions (b); random spread gives each annotator independent samples, leaving too little shared overlap for reliable estimation; \revised{Stratified shared overlap draws a proportional stratum sample that all annotators label, simultaneously fixing fragmentation (maximal pairwise co-coverage) and representativeness (stratum-proportional distribution).}
abstract: Validating an LLM-as-a-judge requires estimating its agreement with humans, yet annotation budgets rarely allow every item to be multiply labeled. We prove that this overlap sparsity is the first-order determinant of wrong deployment decisions: at 5% pairwise overlap, wrong-decision rates reach 25% and the probability of selecting the wrong best judge among ten candidates is 65%. The two actionable levers are overlap quantity and allocation. For quantity, we derive a minimum-overlap formula showing $Ï\geq 0.25$ suffices for non-borderline judges while borderline cases remain fundamentally hard. For allocation, a zero-cost stratified scheme halves false-rejection rates relative to random sampling when strata are informative. We validate on 10 LLM judges across four evaluation matrices spanning visual assessment, causal reasoning, and summarization.
